source_text: »Ἀποκριθεὶς δὲ Ἰησοῦς· ἀμὴν ὑμῖν λέγω. ὃς ἂν ἀφῇ τὰ ἴδια καὶ γονεῖς καὶ ἀδελφοὺς καὶ χρήματα ἕνεκεν ἐμοῦ καὶ ἕνεκεν τοῦ εὐαγγελίου. ἀπολήψεται ἑκατονταπλασίονα.« ἀλλὰ μηδὲ τοῦθ᾿ ἡμᾶς ἐπιταρασσέτω μηδὲ τὸ ἔτι τούτου σκληρότερον ἀλλαχοῦ ταῖς φωναῖς ἐξενηνεγμένον· »ὅς οὐ μισεῖ πατέρα καὶ μητέρα καὶ παῖδας. προσέτι δὲ καὶ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχήν, ἐμὸς μαθητὴς εἶναι οὐ δύναται.« οὐ γὰρ εἰσηγεῖται μῖσος καὶ διάλυσιν ἀπὸ τῶν φιλτάτων ὁ τῆς εἰρήνης θεός. ὅ γε καὶ τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ἀγαπᾶν παραινῶν. εἰ δὲ τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ἀγαπητέον, ἀνάλογον ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνων ἀνιόντι καὶ τοὺς ἐγγυτάτω γένους· ἢ εἰ μισητέον τοὺς πρὸς αἵματος, πολὺ μᾶλλον τοὺς ἐχθροὺς προβάλλεσθαι κατιὼν ὁ λόγος διδάσκει, ὥστε ἀλλήλους ἀναιροῦντες ἐλέγχοιντ᾿ ἂν οἱ λόγοι. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ἀναιροῦσιν οὐδ᾿ ἐγγύς, ἀπὸ γὰρ τῆς αὐτῆς γνώμης καὶ διαθέσεως καὶ ἐπὶ τῷ αὐτῷ ὅρῳ πατέρα μισοίη τις ἂν καὶ ἐχθρὸν ἀγαπώῃ ὁ μήτε ἐχθρὸν ἀμυνόμενος μήτε πατέρα Χριστοῦ πλέον αἰδούμενος. ἐν ἐκείνῳ μὲν γὰρ τῷ λόγῳ μῖσος ἐκκόπτει καὶ κακοποιίαν, ἐν τούτῳ δὲ τὴν πρὸς τὰ σύντροφα δυσωπίαν. εἰ βλάπτοι πρὸς σωτηρίαν, εἰ γοῦν ἄθεος εἴη τινὶ πατὴρ ἢ υἱὸς ἢ ἀδελφὸς καὶ κώλυμα τῆς πίστεως γένοιτο καὶ ἐμπόδιον τῆς ἄνω ζωῆς, τούτῳ μὴ συμφερέσθω μηδὲ ὁμονοείτω. ἀλλὰ τὴν σαρκικὴν οἰκειότητα διὰ τὴν πνευματικὴν ἔχθραν διαλυσάτω.
thought_title: The two sayings on leaving and hating kin are reconciled
orientation: Clement is interpreting Jesus' hard sayings about leaving family and hating father and mother, showing they do not command real hatred but a right ordering of loves.
pass_a_gloss: And Jesus answered: Truly I say to you, whoever leaves his own things and parents and brothers and money for my sake and for the sake of the gospel, will receive a hundredfold. But let not even this disturb us, nor the still harder saying uttered elsewhere in the words: He who does not hate father and mother and children, and in addition even his own soul, cannot be my disciple. For the God of peace does not introduce hatred and separation from those dearest, he who indeed urges loving even enemies. But if enemies must be loved, by analogy going up from those also the nearest of kin; or if those of one's blood must be hated, much more would the argument going down teach to put forward enemies, so that the arguments, refuting each other, would be convicted. But they do not refute, nor come near, for from the same mind and disposition and on the same boundary one might hate a father and love an enemy, the one who neither defends against an enemy nor reverences a father more than Christ. For in that saying he cuts out hatred and wrongdoing, but in this one the shame before those brought up together. If it should harm toward salvation, if indeed a father or son or brother should be godless to someone and become a hindrance of faith and an obstacle of the life above, let him not join with this one nor be of one mind. But let him dissolve the fleshly kinship because of the spiritual enmity.

choices.why: Literal rendering of the neuter plural possessive, matching the source's vagueness about what is left
Standard literal rendering of the multiplicative adjective
Preserves the third-person imperative force of the source
Captures the sense of reverential shame or awe before close relations that Clement says must be cut out

Preserves the third-person imperative and the strong verb of breaking apart

pass_b_english: Jesus answered, “Truly I tell you, whoever leaves his own things and parents and brothers and money for my sake and for the sake of the gospel will receive back a hundredfold” (Mark 10:29-30). But let this not disturb us, nor the still harsher saying uttered elsewhere in the words: “Whoever does not hate father and mother and children, and even his own soul, cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26). For the God of peace is not introducing hatred and separation from those most loved—he who urges us to love even our enemies. If enemies must be loved, then by the same reasoning, moving upward from them, so must those nearest in family; or if those of one's own blood must be hated, then the saying, moving downward, teaches that enemies must be hated far more, so that the two sayings would be shown to refute each other. But they do not refute each other, nor come close. For from the same mind and disposition and on the same principle a person would hate a father and love an enemy—one who neither takes revenge on an enemy nor reverences a father more than Christ. In the one saying he cuts out hatred and wrongdoing; in the other, the deference toward intimates. If it harms salvation—if, say, a father or son or brother is godless to someone and becomes a hindrance to faith and an obstacle to the life above—let him not join with that one or be of one mind with him, but let him dissolve the fleshly kinship because of the spiritual enmity.

problems.source_quote: »Ἀποκριθεὶς δὲ Ἰησοῦς· ἀμὴν ὑμῖν λέγω. ὃς ἂν ἀφῇ τὰ ἴδια καὶ γονεῖς καὶ ἀδελφοὺς καὶ χρήματα ἕνεκεν ἐμοῦ καὶ ἕνεκεν τοῦ εὐαγγελίου. ἀπολήψεται ἑκατονταπλασίονα.«
problems.why: The citation Mark 10:29-30 is wrong; this matches Mark 10:29 but lacks 'lands' and 'persecutions' of v.30, and the source's single verse better fits Mark 10:29 alone or Matthew 19:29/Luke 18:29.
problems.ruling: Greek quote lacks lands/persecutions; not verbatim Mark 10:29‑30, so citation misleads.

problems.why: Greek says "more ashamed" (πλέον αἰδούμενος), not "more than Christ"; adds a comparison that isn’t in the source.
problems.fix: …who neither defends an enemy nor honors his father, being more ashamed.
problems.ruling: πατέρα Χριστοῦ πλέον αἰδούμενος = 'honoring father more than Christ,' not 'more ashamed'; 'more than Christ' misreads πλέον as modifying αἰδούμενος rather than comparing father to Christ.

edits.old: nor honors a father more than Christ
edits.new: nor honors a father, being more ashamed

fixed: Citation corrected to Mark 10:29; the source quotation matches Mark 10:29 alone, lacking the additional elements of v.30.

The Greek πατέρα Χριστοῦ πλέον αἰδούμενος means 'reverencing a father more than Christ' is a misreading; πλέον modifies αἰδούμενος, so the sense is 'being more ashamed' rather than a comparison with Christ. The English now reflects this.

problems.source_quote: μήτε ἐχθρὸν ἀμυνόμενος μήτε πατέρα Χριστοῦ πλέον αἰδούμενος
problems.why: Misreads αἰδούμενος as 'being ashamed' rather than 'showing reverence/respect'; should be 'revering Christ more'.
problems.fix: one who neither takes revenge on an enemy nor reverences a father more than Christ
problems.ruling: αἰδόμενος = reverent/respectful, not ‘ashamed’; translation ‘being more ashamed’ misrepresents meaning.

problems.quote: the shame felt before those brought up together
problems.why: Misreads δυσωπίαν as 'shame' rather than 'deference/respect'; σύντροφα means 'intimates/family', not 'those brought up together'.
problems.ruling: δυσωπίαν = double‑facedness/hypocrisy, not ‘shame’; σύντροφα = companions/intimates, not ‘those brought up together’.

edits.old: one who neither takes revenge on an enemy nor honors a father, being more ashamed.
edits.new: one who neither takes revenge on an enemy nor reverences a father more than Christ.

edits.old: the shame felt before those brought up together.

fixed: mistranslation: 'being more ashamed' misreads αἰδούμενος as 'being ashamed' rather than 'showing reverence/respect'; the source is 'μήτε ἐχθρὸν ἀμυνόμενος μήτε πατέρα Χριστοῦ πλέον αἰδούμενος', meaning 'neither taking revenge on an enemy nor reverencing a father more than Christ'. Fixed to 'reverences a father more than Christ'.

mistranslation: 'the shame felt before those brought up together' misreads δυσωπίαν as 'shame' rather than 'deference/respect', and σύντροφα as 'those brought up together' rather than 'intimates/family'. The source is 'τὴν πρὸς τὰ σύντροφα δυσωπίαν', meaning 'the deference toward intimates'. Fixed to 'the deference toward intimates'.

problems.why: συμφερέσθω means 'agree with/join with'; correct. No error.
The quoted promise of a hundredfold is from Mark 10:30, not 10:29.
problems.ruling: Mark 10:29 lists what is left; 10:30 contains 'hundredfold' reward. Source lacks chapter/verse; English adds wrong reference.

fixed: join with: συμφερέσθω means 'agree with/join with'; the English is correct.
Scripture reference: the hundredfold promise is in Mark 10:30, not 10:29; corrected.

fixed.note: The quotation starts in 10:29 ('Truly I tell you, whoever leaves...') and ends in 10:30 ('hundredfold'), so neither verse alone is right.

dismissed.why: δυσωπίαν means shame/reluctance to offend, not 'deference'; 'intimates' for σύντροφα (those raised together/family) is weak.
dismissed.note: δυσωπία here is the bashful deference that gives way to one's own people, so 'deference toward intimates' is a fair rendering.
